0.note: Namaskaaram is a complete conventional greeting. Learn it as a word, rather than treating each syllable as a separate meaning.

1.note: Nandi is a complete thank-you. Malayalam does not need a separate word for “you” in this expression.

2.literal: Well-being + is / are …? → Are you well?
2.note: Sukham means comfort, health or well-being, borrowed from Sanskrit sukha (“ease / happiness”). Aano is the question form of aanu (“is / are”): aanu + -o. The listener is understood, so no separate “you” is needed.

3.note: This is the short, natural answer to sukhamaano? The person and “am” are understood from the conversation.

4.note: Ente is the possessive of njaan (“I”). Put ente before peru (“name”), then give your name. English needs “is”; this short introduction can leave it understood.

5.literal: Tomorrow + can / let us see. → See you tomorrow.
5.note: Naale sets the time. Kaanaam is from kaanuka (“see”); in a goodbye it means “see you / let us meet”, not simply “I can see”.

6.note: Oru before a noun can mean “one” or “a”. Put what you want before venam. The person is understood: the whole phrase naturally becomes “I’d like a tea”.

7.note: Vellam names the thing you want; venam supplies the want / need. Malayalam can omit “I” when the order is obviously yours.

8.note: The pattern is oru + item + venam. Swap kaappi for another drink while keeping the order the same.

9.note: Kattan describes the kind of tea. Learn it as a tea-shop expression meaning tea without milk; it does not literally contain a separate word for “without”.

10.note: Paal names the thing being declined. Venda is the negative want / need form. Compare paal venam (“I want milk”) with paal venda (“no milk”).

11.note: Madhuram means sweetness / sweetening. In a tea order, this asks for no sugar or sweetening. Venda declines it; the polite “please” comes from tone and context.

12.note: Evide is already a question word. It does not need the yes/no ending -o. Point or name the place you are asking about.

13.note: Keep the familiar borrowed place expression bus stand, then add evide. The linking “is” and article “the” in English are understood.

14.note: Use the familiar place name before evide. You can reuse this question with another place: [place] evide?

15.note: Ivide tells the driver where. Nirthu is an instruction from nirththuka (“stop”); the native form has a long final vowel. Do not confuse ivide (“here”) with evide (“where”).

16.note: The base for the left side changes shape to idath-/edath- before the direction ending -ottu. Learn the joined direction edathottu as a unit you can say quickly.

17.note: Valam (“right side”) uses the changed stem valath- before -ottu (“towards”). The result is a direction, rather than a description of something on your right.

18.note: Ethra asks for an amount; roopa names the currency. No -o is needed because ethra already makes this an information question.

19.note: Venam can stand alone when the offered item is obvious. Enikku … venam is the fuller pattern for “I want / need …”.

20.note: Venda is a complete way to decline an offered item. Learn venam and venda as a contrasting pair; do not construct the negative by adding a separate English-style “not”.

21.note: Ithu stands for the object you point to. In the fuller form enikku ithu venam, enikku identifies who wants it; here it can be left out.

22.note: Kurachu limits the amount. Kuraykk- is the reduce / lower stem; the questioned -aam form makes a possible-action request. The final -o asks the question, but does not itself mean “please”.

23.note: Tharu- is giving towards the speaker. Tharum (“will give”) becomes tharumo? with the question ending -o. As a request, natural English is “Could I have the bill?”.

24.literal: In the mind + became clear + not.
24.note: Manassilaayi is “understood”. The negative past form joins the changed past stem with -illa: manassilaayilla. Learn the positive and negative together; this is not the present “I don’t know”.

25.note: Veendum tells how to repeat the action. Paray- is the say / speak stem; the -aam form plus question ending -o makes a polite request.

26.literal: A little / just + slowly + could [you] speak?
26.note: Onnu literally means “one”, but before a request it often softens it to “just / a little”. Pathukke describes speaking slowly; the final verb asks for the action.

27.note: Ariyilla is the negative knowing form. The person is understood. Add enikku to say explicitly “I don’t know”.

28.note: Malayalam often expresses knowing with a “to / for” person form. Enikku names the experiencer, Malayalam is what is known, and ariyilla supplies the negative.

29.note: Ariyaam means “know”; ariyaamo? asks whether someone knows. The person is understood from context, so this naturally means “Do you know English?”.

30.note: Sahaayikk- is the help stem. The long -oo ending makes a request / instruction. Tone and context supply the polite “please”.

31.note: Aashupathri names the place, then evide asks its location. The natural English question adds “is the”.

32.note: Marunnu names what is needed. Venam can express need as well as want; in this situation “I need medicine” is natural.

33.note: Marunnu kada is a medicine shop: a pharmacy. Then evide asks where it is. This is a useful example of two ordinary words naming a place.

34.note: Enikku identifies who experiences the pain. Vayar names the stomach and vedana is pain. This is a short spoken expression, with the existence / have relation understood.

35.note: Enikku (“to me”) + pani (“fever”) + undu (“exists”) naturally becomes “I have a fever”. Undu is used for existence / possession; it is different from the identity-linking aanu.

42.note: Kandathil refers to having seen / met someone. Together with santhosham (“happiness”), this is the conventional “Nice to meet you”.

45.literal: We (excluding you) + here + for the first time + is.
45.note: Njangal excludes the listener. Aadyamaayi means “for the first time”; aanu can join to focus it. Natural English reorganizes this as “It is our first time here”.

71.note: Vazhi thetti is the everyday expression for losing your way. Enikku identifies the person affected; natural English uses “I have lost my way”.

76.literal: This + put on and + may I try / see?
76.note: Ittu links putting the item on to nokkaamo (“may I look / try?”). Together these actions make the ordinary expression for trying on clothing.

80.literal: This + to me + liking came to be.
80.note: Ishtamaayi means that something became liked / pleasing. With enikku, the natural English is “I like this one / I liked this”.

84.note: Padikkuka is the learning / studying verbal-noun form. Aanu joins with a linking y in the ongoing-action expression padikkukayaanu: “am learning”.

88.literal: What I said + correct + is it?
88.note: Paranjathu turns “said” into “what was said”. Shariyaano asks whether that is correct. Natural English is “Did I say that correctly?”.

121.literal: UPI + by way of + money + can [I] send?
121.note: Vazhi (“way / route”) works here as “through / by”. The send-verb request asks whether payment through UPI is possible.

134.note: Oorano is the questioned necessity form of the remove verb. It asks whether removing footwear is required, rather than whether you are able to remove it.

141.literal: Backwater / lake + trip + book + may [I] do?
141.note: An English activity word can combine with cheyyuka (“do”) to make a Malayalam verb. Book cheyyaamo? asks whether you can book the trip.

61.note: Idaamo literally asks “could you put / set [it]?”. With the fare meter, it asks the driver to switch it on and charge by it. Here meter is the fare device, rather than a distance unit.

parts.meaning: put; set; switch on in this context
